problem_framing.rationale: The document answers the question as posed (whether to raise, and how) with a by-segment answer in the governing thought. It uses the 15% growth target ($12.9M) and NRR above 100% as explicit columns in the options table, and honours the renewal-timing and enterprise-contract constraints in both the sizing and the plan. The issues the answer turns on (promotion mix effect, the reachable prize, Inkwell in SMB, mid-market headroom) appear in the executive summary. Overall NRR is never computed and the NRR criterion is applied only qualitatively, but that is minor.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the four executive-summary points map one-to-one to the sections, and nearly every title is a claim its slide supports; the titles alone give the argument. Two tension points remain. Slide 10's title frames the 2023 rise negatively ("left it higher than before", a 0.1 pp difference), yet its body says the core tolerated it and the plan reuses 8% as the SMB test level. Slide 13's title jumps from a new-sign-up test to "the tested level for renewals", which its own footnote walks back. "Activation, not price, is the lever" also sits awkwardly beside a title saying the cohort left over price.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-derived every figure and found no numerical errors: 96% and 74% shares, blended churn 1.7%→2.6% and 0.8%→1.2%, the 1.0/0.1 pp decomposition, $7.566M reachable, $65.5M (76%) renewing, $4.27M targeted, $16.6M × 8% = $1.3M, and the 32% cohort-fix cut. All five critical evidence items are used, including the cohort split of the exit survey and the caps. The flaws are in what was not done and in overstated wording. The 2023 precedent is costed (~$0.6M lost) but never netted against the 8% uplift, and no break-even churn is computed, so the slide reads more negative than the evidence. The implied ~4.9% promotion-cohort churn is not stated. "Tested price levels" is overstated: the test covered new mid-market sign-ups only, and enterprise at 10% was never tested. "Activation, not price, is the lever" is a causal claim from a correlation. No churn response is netted into the $4.3M, though this is disclosed.

strategic_judgment.rationale: The recommendation is clear, differentiated by segment and follows from the analysis. Three options are compared on the stated objectives, the $3.3M given up against the CFO plan is made explicit, the onboarding halving claim is discounted to a one-third best case, and there is an SMB holdout test with a Q2 go/no-go, a churn guardrail and owned next steps. It avoids the main traps. Shortfalls: the go/no-go criteria are deferred ("roll out if churn holds") with no break-even threshold to anchor them; the mid-market guardrail of 0.8% a month is loosely specified; no lower-priced tier or grandfathering is considered as a response to Inkwell; and the 67% of the growth target not covered by pricing is acknowledged but left unaddressed.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: The answer is on the second page, the language is plain and the derivations are shown inline. Nineteen slides include four section dividers, a title and a next-steps page, so about eleven carry content, which is roughly proportionate. There is some repetition (the discount-expiry timing appears on slides 5 and 6; the advisory-board and Inkwell-above-200-seats points recur) and a few loose phrasings ("enterprise caps limit the rest", "never set the product up").

unsupported_claims.quote: A 10% higher price did not measurably slow mid-market sign-ups in 2024, making it the tested level for renewals
unsupported_claims.why: The 2024 test covered new sign-ups only; it does not test renewals. The footnote admits this is an open question, but the title asserts it.

unsupported_claims.quote: Mid-market and enterprise renewals alone would add about $4.3M of ARR in 2027 at tested price levels
unsupported_claims.why: No enterprise price test is in the pack (10% on uncapped enterprise is untested), and the mid-market level was tested on sign-ups, not renewals.

unsupported_claims.quote: Activation, not price, is the lever: low-activity new customers churn about three times as often
unsupported_claims.why: This is a causal claim from a correlation. The pack lists whether the cohort can be activated as an open uncertainty, and 52% of promotion churners cite price.

unsupported_claims.quote: customers who stay for integrations and the audit trail face real switching costs at renewal
unsupported_claims.why: Switching costs are not in the pack; this is inferred from advisory-board stated reasons for staying.

unsupported_claims.quote: Promotion customers never set the product up
unsupported_claims.why: 41% of the promotion cohort did reach five documents in month one; the title turns a lower activation rate into an absolute.

unsupported_claims.quote: 85% of mid-market and 40% of enterprise ARR renew in 2027, as the renewal calendar shows
unsupported_claims.why: The figures are from the pack, but no renewal calendar exists there; the source is invented.

recommendation.summary: Raise by segment: mid-market +10% at renewal and enterprise up to the 7% cap (10% where uncapped) from January 2027, for about $4.3M before churn. Hold SMB in January, run an 8% renewal test on non-promotion SMB against a holdout with a go/no-go at end of Q2 2027, and reprice the promotion cohort only after an activation programme. Reject both the CFO's uniform 12% and a full price hold.
recommendation.rationale: It meets all four defensibility criteria. It separates the mix effect (1.0 pp) from the rate effect (0.1 pp). It reconciles the CFO and CEO views: the churn rise is a promotion-cohort effect, but those customers leave over price and Inkwell makes SMB exposed. It corrects $10.3M to $7.6M. It differentiates pricing by segment with a staged SMB test and a churn guardrail.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The document neither adopts nor rejects the CFO's view wholesale. It confirms that the churn rise is mostly a promotion mix effect (91% of the SMB rise; non-promotion churn 2.0%→2.1%), which supports the CFO's diagnosis. It also shows the cohort left over price at discount expiry (52% against 18%) and that Inkwell has cut the SMB win rate, which supports the CEO's concern for SMB. It corrects the $10.3M to $7.6M for renewal timing and caps and replaces the uniform 12% with a by-segment plan. It flags the sign-up-versus-renewal uncertainty, the missing survey sample sizes, the unevidenced halving claim and the undefined dashboard metric. The one overreach is the causal claim that activation rather than price is the lever.

output.overall_comment: Strong, accurate work with a weighted score of about 4.15. Every number I re-derived matches the pack, all critical evidence is used, and the recommendation is a defensible differentiated increase with a staged SMB test. The main gaps are: no break-even or net read of the 2023 precedent, so that slide is framed more negatively than the evidence; "tested" wording that overstates what the 2024 sign-up test shows, especially for enterprise; go/no-go criteria that are deferred rather than specified; and no consideration of a lower-priced tier or grandfathering against Inkwell. The gap to the 15% growth target is acknowledged but not addressed.
